EITC CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's your Earned Income Tax Credit worth?

The federal Earned Income Tax Credit is worth up to $8,231 depending on how many qualifying children you have and how much you earn — but it phases IN with earned income, plateaus at a maximum, then phases OUT again, and IRS Publication 596's own worksheet computes it twice (once from earned income, once from AGI) and keeps the smaller result. This applies the phase-in/phase-out formula, the investment income limit, and the AGI comparison.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status & income

Fill in filing status, income, and qualifying children, then click Calculate.

Estimate

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This estimates the EITC only — not your total tax liability, other deductions or credits, or state tax (many states offer their own EITC on top of the federal one).
  • Age, residency, relationship, and investment income are self-reported — this tool does not verify any of them.
  • Qualifying-child tests (relationship, residency, age, joint-return) are assumed already met — this tool does not determine who counts as a qualifying child.
  • Federal only. Most states with their own EITC compute it as a percentage of the federal credit — check your state.

Common questions

How much is the Earned Income Tax Credit?

Up to $664 with no qualifying children, $4,427 with one child, $7,316 with two children, or $8,231 with three or more children, for 2026. The credit phases in with earned income, plateaus at the maximum, then phases out at higher income -- see the phase-out question below.

Does the credit depend on earned income or AGI?

Both. IRS Publication 596's own EIC Worksheet method computes the credit twice -- once using earned income, once using adjusted gross income (AGI) -- with the identical phase-in/plateau/phase-out formula, and the final credit is the SMALLER of the two results. A filer with low earned income but higher AGI (investment income under the limit, unemployment, a working spouse) can be phased out by AGI even though an earned-income-only lookup would suggest a larger credit -- the detail a hand calculation almost always misses.

What is the investment income limit?

$12,200 for 2026. If investment income (interest, dividends, capital gains, rental income) exceeds that limit, the EITC is disallowed entirely, regardless of how low earned income or AGI is.

Can I claim the EITC with no qualifying children?

Yes, but only if the filer (or, on a joint return, at least one spouse) is age 25 through 64 at year-end, is not claimed as a dependent, and lived in the US more than half the year.

Can I claim it if I file married filing separately?

Generally no. The one exception: a qualifying child lived with you more than half the year AND you lived apart from your spouse for the last six months of the year (or are legally separated). That narrow case is treated like a single filer, using the single/head-of-household phase-out thresholds rather than the higher joint ones.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published statutory amounts, phase-in/phase-out formula, and eligibility rules to the numbers and checkboxes you enter. It is not a full tax return, does not verify age, residency, or relationship, and is not a substitute for reviewing the IRS's own guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own age, residency, relationship, and income figures before filing. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also checking the Child Tax Credit for the same return? See the Child Tax Credit calculator — a separate, stackable federal credit with its own $2,200-per-child amount and phase-out, unrelated to the EITC's earned-income-based formula.

Estimating this by hand instead? See where a hand calculation of this credit usually goes wrong.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. working out the EITC by hand

The headline numbers — up to $8,231 with three or more children — are easy to find. The part that goes wrong by hand is the two-lookup rule, the investment income cliff, and the narrow married-filing- separately exception.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Earned income vs. AGILooks the credit up from earned income only and stops.Computes the credit from BOTH earned income and AGI and keeps the smaller, per IRS Publication 596's own worksheet.
Investment income limitForgets it entirely, or treats it as a phase-out instead of a flat disqualifier.Checks investment income against the $12,200 limit first and zeroes the credit outright if it's exceeded.
Phase-out threshold by child countAssumes the threshold rises with each additional child.Uses the same threshold for 1, 2, or 3+ children -- only the phase-out RATE and ceiling differ.
Married filing separatelyAssumes MFS always disqualifies the EITC.Checks for the living-apart-with-a-qualifying-child exception before disqualifying.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Looking the credit up from earned income only and stopping there. IRS Publication 596's own EIC Worksheet computes the credit a second time from AGI and keeps the SMALLER of the two -- so a filer with modest earned income but higher AGI (investment income under the limit, unemployment, a working spouse on a joint return) can get a materially smaller credit than an earned-income-only lookup would suggest.

What's the second most common mistake?

Forgetting the investment income limit entirely. A filer can have low earned income and qualify for a large credit by the phase-in/phase-out math alone, and still be disqualified outright because investment income (interest, dividends, capital gains, rental income) exceeds $12,200 for 2026 -- a flat disqualifier, not a phase-out.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Using the wrong phase-out threshold for the number of children. The phase-out threshold is the SAME dollar figure for 1, 2, or 3+ children ($23,890 single, $31,160 joint for 2026) -- only the 0-children category has its own, lower threshold. It is the phase-OUT RATE and the completed-phaseout ceiling that differ by child count, not the threshold where phase-out begins.

What eligibility mistake gets made most often?

Assuming married filing separately always disqualifies the EITC. It generally does -- but a filer with a qualifying child who lived with them more than half the year, who also lived apart from their spouse for the last six months of the year (or is legally separated), can still claim it as if single. A hand check that stops at "MFS means no EITC" misses this narrow but real exception.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page computes your total tax liability, verifies the qualifying-child tests, or models a state EITC. Both apply the same published federal phase-in/phase-out formula and eligibility rules to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS Publication 596 or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal EITC rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
